𝐓𝐂𝐒 𝐐𝟐 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕: 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐬. 𝐁𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬. 𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐈𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡?

Tata Consultancy Services closed Q2 FY27 with a familiar IT-services story: 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠, 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐦𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝.

Revenue came in at $𝟕.𝟔𝟒𝐁, 𝐮𝐩 𝟎.𝟐% 𝐐𝐨𝐐 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝟐.𝟒% 𝐘𝐨𝐘, 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐭-𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐚𝐭 𝟎.𝟓% 𝐐𝐨𝐐 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝟐.𝟖% 𝐘𝐨𝐘.

Yet the company 𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝟐𝟒% 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝟏𝟗% 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧, 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐚𝐭 𝟏𝟎𝟐.𝟐% 𝐨𝐟 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭.

The interesting part is demand.

#TCS closed the quarter with a $𝟗.𝟔𝐁 𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐓𝐂𝐕, 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐝𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝟐 𝐜𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟏𝟎𝐌+ 𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐨𝐫𝐲, 𝟔 𝐢𝐧 $𝟓𝐌+ 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝟏𝟏 𝐢𝐧 $𝟏𝐌+.

So why doesn't revenue growth look stronger?

𝐁𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐠𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬.

Large transformation contracts need mobilisation, hiring, transition and implementation before they reach full billing. The ramp-up of large deals, including BSNL, therefore becomes just as important as the headline TCV itself.

There is another critical aspect influencing the revenue numbers.

AI is creating demand while simultaneously putting pressure on the traditional IT-services revenue model.

AI-led productivity can mean more work gets delivered with fewer hours, creating pricing and revenue pressure even as enterprise AI spending increases.

That helps explain TCS' current “low growth, high profit” equation.

The growth picture is also uneven.

#BFSI, TCS' largest vertical at 32.8% of revenue, grew 2.5% QoQ in constant currency. Manufacturing and Technology & Services both grew 3.1%.

Meanwhile, Consumer Business declined 0.7%, and Regional Markets & Others declined 5.8% QoQ CC.

Geographically, North America still contributes 48.3% of revenue, while the UK grew 3.5% QoQ CC. India, however, declined 10.3% QoQ CC.

And TCS continues to invest heavily in the capability required for this new environment: 367K+ associates now have higher proficiency in AI/ML, supported by 31.8M learning hours YTD.

The real question for TCS isn't whether it can win large deals.

It clearly can.

The question is:

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐲 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐚𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐀𝐈 𝐢𝐬 𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐞𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐥𝐲 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐜𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲?

That may be the defining brand factor for TCS over the next few quarters.

It’s October. India is gearing up for Navratri, Dussehra, and Diwali.
Festive music is in the air, consumer spending is peaking, and yet... my feed is filled with "I was laid off today" posts.

What’s even more alarming? A lot of these professionals were hired just 2 to 3 months ago.

Some had barely completed onboarding. Others were still in their probation period.
If companies spent millions recruiting them weeks ago, why let them go right before the festive season?

It feels completely illogical from the outside, but inside corporate boardrooms, it comes down to cold financial timing:

1️⃣ Q3 Fiscal Adjustments: September 30 marks the end of Q3 for global MNCs (and Q2 for Indian financial calendars). When revenue targets are missed, cost-cutting directives hit immediately in early October to protect year-end margins.

2️⃣ The Probation Catch-22: Employees on probation (typically 0–6 months) are contractually the easiest to let go. They require shorter notice periods, minimal severance, and low operational risk to drop.

3️⃣ Client Contract Delays: A lot of lateral hiring happens on "projected" client deals. If a European or US client pauses or cancels a pipeline in late Q3, the bench that was created for it gets eliminated overnight.

4️⃣ Shift to Profitability & Automation: Across tech and IT, companies are restructuring budgets toward AI and automation while trimming redundant operational roles.

It’s a stark reminder: A job offer or a recent join date is not an indicator of job security.

To anyone affected by this recent wave right before the holidays: Please remember this is a reflection of corporate financial planning, not your skill or worth.

If you or anyone in your network has been impacted recently, drop a comment below or reach out directly. Let’s use this platform to help connect people with teams that are actually hiring.

In my work with companies to thoughtfully implement AI, I often observe companies implementing AI with no one responsible for oversight. 

When companies take on a new kind of risk, there’s usually a playbook. Someone gets assigned responsibility for it. Sometimes a committee forms to oversee it. There’s ongoing monitoring, because the risk doesn’t go away after the first review, it has to be watched over time. That’s how most businesses handle cybersecurity, compliance, even workplace safety. 

Yet, at most companies I work with, AI hasn’t received that treatment. Instead, AI decisions get scattered. IT picks the tools. Legal worries about the contracts. Compliance worries about the regulations. HR worries about how it touches employees. Everyone assumes someone else is watching the whole picture, and the result is that no one actually is. 

This isn’t about hiring a Chief AI Officer or setting up a massive new function. It’s about applying the same structure you already use for other risks: a clear owner, and a process for ongoing monitoring and development. 

A few things worth asking yourself this week: 
→ If an employee wants to adopt a new AI tool, who approves it? 
→ If an AI tool makes a mistake that affects a customer or employee, who finds out first, and what happens next? 
→ Is there one person or committee responsible for AI decisions company-wide, or is it scattered across departments? 
→ Does leadership actually know what’s being decided, or is it happening quietly at the team level? 

If the answer to any of these is “I’m not sure,” that’s usually the first sign the structure needs tightening before the policy does. 

This is part of a series on the practical side of AI adoption, not the hype. The goal isn’t to slow AI down, it’s to help you use it well. 

At McLane Middleton, I work with companies to thoughtfully implement AI.

‼️ 🧠 BREAKING: Washington Just Put Big Tech’s Talent Model Under Review — Microsoft’s PERM Suspension Raises a New Labor-Cost Risk

Microsoft’s PERM suspension is more than an immigration-policy issue—it adds workforce-planning and labor-cost risk for tech companies dependent on employer-sponsored permanent residency.

The action also reaches beyond Microsoft. 

Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling also named Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCLTech and Capgemini amid active federal investigations. A PERM suspension can halt new employer-sponsored green-card filings during a probe.

🔴 Microsoft faces a workforce-planning overhang: A PERM suspension does not automatically cancel existing approvals or H-1B status, but it can constrain future retention planning for skilled employees seeking permanent residency. That elevates uncertainty around hiring, internal mobility and replacement costs.

🟠 The risk is wider for IT-services vendors: Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant and Capgemini operate labor-intensive delivery models. Any prolonged restriction on permanent-residency sponsorship could increase onshore staffing costs, accelerate localization requirements and pressure utilization economics.

🔵 Labor arbitrage is now a policy target: The administration is framing enforcement around alleged abuse, wage suppression and displacement of U.S. workers. For investors, that shifts the debate from visa availability to the durability of labor-cost advantages embedded in global technology-services business models.

🟢 Margin protection may require repricing: If companies must hire more U.S.-based talent, raise domestic compensation or absorb higher retention costs, the next transmission mechanism is commercial: higher bill rates, narrower gross margins, or both.

🟡 Clients will not automatically absorb the increase: Enterprise IT budgets remain disciplined. Vendors with differentiated AI, cybersecurity, cloud-modernization or mission-critical capabilities may have room to pass through inflation. Lower-value, labor-heavy outsourcing contracts are likely to face greater margin compression.

⚫ This is a governance and valuation event as much as a labor-policy event: The immediate financial hit may be limited if existing approvals remain intact. The larger issue is whether federal scrutiny becomes persistent, broad-based and restrictive enough to reset long-term cost assumptions across U.S. technology and IT outsourcing.

For Microsoft, the direct earnings effect is likely less material than for the Indian IT-services complex, given its scale, product mix and pricing power. But the reputational and execution risk is meaningful: immigration compliance has moved closer to the center of corporate workforce strategy.

The bigger opportunity is changing how we think about talent altogether.
Look globally.  

Hire for capability, not just credentials.  

Build a mix of permanent employees, contractors and project-based teams.
  
Use AI to make strong people even more productive.  

And when it makes sense, stop buying hours and start buying outcomes.

Sometimes you need to hire the person.
Sometimes you need specialized expertise for six months.
Sometimes you just need the project delivered.

The answer shouldn’t always be “add headcount.”

India's sovereign AI bet has just hired one of Big Tech's most senior India executives.

Sarvam AI has brought in Sashikumar Sreedharan, who until this week was Managing Director of Google Cloud India, as President and Chief Business Officer, according to multiple reports. Google Cloud has named Amit Kumar, head of its Digital Natives business in India, as interim India lead.

What Sarvam does
Bengaluru-based Sarvam, co-founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar, is building a full-stack sovereign AI platform for India: foundation models such as Sarvam 105B and the edge-focused Sarvam 30B, speech and vision models for Indian languages, and conversational, agentic and inference platforms for enterprises, governments and developers.

Key numbers
• $234M raised in the first close of a $300M Series B (June 2026)
• $1.5B post-money valuation
• HCLTech the lead strategic investor with $150M; Bessemer joined, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV continued
• Sarvam Vision has digitised 35M+ pages; its speech models transcribe 5 lakh+ hours of audio a month (company figures)

Who is joining
Sreedharan led Google Cloud India as MD from July 2025, after about two years as Google Cloud's APAC COO. Earlier, he led Microsoft India's enterprise commercial business and was CEO and MD of Happiest Minds Technologies.

Why it matters
Indian AI labs are moving from research to revenue, and that needs leaders who know how large enterprises and governments buy technology. Hiring a former hyperscaler country head signals Sarvam is gearing up to compete for big enterprise and public-sector contracts. His start date has not been disclosed.
